title: UX Research Starts with Tasks
intro: A full task analysis exposes every decision point in a workflow, but it is slow. Calabro's shortcut is a **Top Task List**: a short, prioritised list of what users are trying to do, built with stakeholders in one working session.

learn.title: Step 1: The most common tasks
learn.text:
A small number of workflows account for most user activity (the 80/20 rule). Find them with **real data**: product analytics, telemetry, click tracking or logs.

Don't guess, and don't ask users to guess either.

try.q: You're building a Top Task List. What is the best source for step 1?
options: Product analytics and usage logs
A stakeholder brainstorm of key features
A survey asking users what they do most
The feature list from the product roadmap
try.explain: Step 1 needs real behaviour data. Guessing, or asking users to guess, is exactly what the method avoids.

learn.title: Step 2: The critical or risky tasks
learn.text:
Some tasks are rare but carry real weight: compliance steps, deadlines, anything essential to the system working.

The test: if something going wrong here would be serious, the task belongs on the list even if it happens once a year.

try.q: A task happens twice a year, but an error means a failed compliance audit. Does it belong on the Top Task List?
options: Yes, as a critical or risky task
No, it is too rare to matter
Only if analytics show growing usage
Only after the common tasks are tested
try.explain: Step 2 adds tasks that are infrequent but high-stakes.

learn.title: Step 3: Dedupe and check coverage
learn.text:
Merge workflows that overlap. When two tasks are alike, keep the one that **touches more screens, UI elements or interaction points**.

You don't need a full task-analysis diagram. The list then feeds every other method: usability tests, walkthroughs and reviews take their scenarios from it.

try.q: Two tasks on your list are nearly the same. Which one do you keep?
options: The one that touches more of the system
The one stakeholders mention more often
The one that is quicker to test
Both, to be safe about coverage
try.explain: Keep the best-representative task: the one covering more screens, elements or interaction points.

test.q: What is a Top Task List?
options: A short, prioritised list of what users are trying to do
A backlog of usability issues ranked by severity and by team
A script of click-by-click test instructions
A list of features ranked by stakeholder votes
test.explain: It is a simplified task analysis: what users try to do, prioritised.

test.q: Why did Calabro create this method instead of always running a full hierarchical task analysis?
options: A full analysis is slow and needs lots of field time
Hierarchical task analysis is no longer a valid research method
Stakeholders refuse to read diagrams
Analytics tools made observation unnecessary
test.explain: He keeps the spirit of formal task analysis but trims it, in the tradition of Nielsen's discount usability.

test.q: What are the three steps, in order?
options: Most common tasks → critical tasks → dedupe and check coverage
Critical tasks → dedupe → most common tasks
User goals → realistic scenario → neutral wording → pilot with one colleague
Recruit users → observe → build a diagram
test.explain: Common first, then critical or risky, then deduplicate.

test.q: Who usually takes part in building the list?
options: The primary stakeholders, in a short working session
Only the research team, working alone
A panel of at least twenty end users
Engineering leads and designers, during regular sprint planning
test.explain: Calabro walks the primary stakeholders through the three steps in a short session.

test.q: What does the finished list change about later research?
options: Studies draw their scenarios from real tasks
Usability tests are no longer needed
Research can skip recruiting real users for most studies
Every feature gets tested equally often
test.explain: The list focuses research; he calls it a multiplier for every other method.
